original_question: Can diabetes medication help alleviate symptoms of a condition caused by an enzyme deficiency that affects ammonia release during metabolism?

final_qi.question: Can diabetes medication help alleviate symptoms of a condition caused by an enzyme deficiency that affects ammonia release during metabolism?
final_qi.long_answer: Yes. The biguanide antidiabetic drug metformin has been reported to lessen hyper-ammonemia and related neurologic symptoms in propionic acidemia, an inborn error caused by propionyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency that leads to excess ammonia release. Metformin activates hepatic AMP-activated protein kinase, up-regulates urea-cycle enzymes and enhances disposal of circulating ammonia, thereby improving the clinical status of patients with this enzyme-deficiency disorder.

final_answer.long_answer: Yes. Metformin, a first-line oral antidiabetic biguanide, has been shown in case reports and experimental studies to lessen hyper-ammonemic episodes in urea-cycle disorders such as ornithine-transcarbamylase deficiency. By inhibiting mitochondrial complex I and glutamate dehydrogenase–driven gluconeogenesis, the drug lowers hepatic production of ammonia; this helps reduce the neurological and gastrointestinal symptoms that arise when the defective enzyme fails to incorporate ammonia into urea.
